source_title: France’s Emmanuel Macron says ‘illegitimate’ protests will be banned as cities block demonstrations
source_excerpt:
French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday that “illegitimate” protests would be banned in the coming days and blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups and vandals for last weekend’s riots and looting.
Speaking after a meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, Macron said demonstrations organized by groups such as trade unions would be allowed to go ahead but could be diverted along alternative routes to protect businesses.
“Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic,” Macron said.
His comments came as authorities across France prepared for fresh protests following some of the country’s worst urban unrest in years.
Authorities in multiple cities had already banned protests planned across the country Thursday.
The turmoil in Paris and other French cities has prompted a strong security response. Night curfews have been implemented in some areas of the French capital, as well as in other cities where calm has been restored.
Demonstrations planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned, a move seen by some as an infringement on French people’s right to protest.
But high school and university student groups say they will continue to mobilize, even though the autumn school break started this week.
The Paris police prefecture said the ban was necessary given the risk of street violence that erupted over the weekend, when groups of masked youths clashed with police forces, looted shops and torched cars.
The ban in Paris will last until 8 p.m. local time and apply to areas including the Élysée presidential palace, both houses of Parliament and the city’s main train stations. Areas in downtown Paris that were severely hit by the looting are also covered.
Thursday’s planned protests were seen as a prelude to Saturday’s big demonstration, when activists from the “yellow vest” movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, are expected to join.
Some of those protests, including marches in Lyon, will also be banned, local authorities said.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who met union representatives Wednesday, said a “massive” security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.
Union representatives said their meeting with Lecornu did not result in concrete proposals. They are now focusing on another big day of action scheduled on Nov. 5 and called on private- and public-sector employees to join.
The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school in Créteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of staff. From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, even in smaller towns.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as complex and unfair.
With the government unable to respond to students’ demands, the school demonstrations and blockades have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before next year’s presidential election to choose Macron’s successor.
